rv.q: This is a strange and surprising yarn, meticulously unspooled.
For all its shagginess, I would recommend seeing The Holes, an imperfect play that still feels groundbreaking.

The Holes wants to have it both ways as a straight drama about gentrification and an absurdist romp about sex, violence, and fragile masculinity, and with a meandering second act, it achieves neither.
It feels like a series of missed opportunities to let go of a gimmick, because the other questions the play asks about community and gentrification and economic survival are vivid and vicious.

cn.t: Critics find this provocative exploration of male loneliness and family obligation compelling, praising its mysterious atmosphere and timely themes about American masculinity and isolation.
